units.title: Physical Quantities and Measurements
units.intro:
Fundamental SI: length m, mass kg, time s, current A, temperature K, amount mol, intensity cd. Derived: speed m/s, force N=kg·m/s². Prefixes: k=10³, c=10⁻², m=10⁻³, μ=10⁻⁶. Convert by multiplying by 1 in disguise (100 cm / 1 m).

Accuracy = close to true. Precision = tight repeats. Significant figures: measured digits you trust. Scientific notation: 3.4×10⁴. Scalar = magnitude only (mass, time, speed). Vector = magnitude + direction (displacement, velocity, force). Add vectors tip-to-tail or by components Fₓ=F cosθ, Fᵧ=F sinθ.

cards.title: 1.1.1 Fundamental and Derived Quantities
body: The building blocks of physics are physical quantities which are used to express the laws of physics.
Length, mass, time, force, speed, temperature, electric charge, and many others are physical quantities.
The three physical quantities - length, mass, and time - serve as fundamental quantities in mechanics - the branch of physics that studies motion and force.
All other quantities that are used in mechanics can be expressed in terms of these three fundamental quantities.

cards.title: 1.1.2 Systems of Measurement
body: In earlier times scientists from different countries were using different systems of units for measurement.
The three systems that were used were: the CGS, the MKS system, and the FPS (or British).
The units of length, mass, and time in the British system are, respectively, foot, slug, and second.

The slug as a unit of mass is not commonly used in the same way the kilogram is used in the SI system, because gravitational force, or weight, is commonly used instead of mass (pound instead of slug) to describe quantities of matter.

cards.title: 1.1.3 Metric (SI) Prefixes
body: For example, the diameter of an atom is 0.000 000 000 54 of a metre.
**A prefix** is a word or syllable that is put in front of a word to add to or change its meaning.
For example, 1/100 of a metre is a centimetre, 1/1000 of a metre is a millimetre and 1000 metres is a kilometre.
The same prefixes are used for other quantities.

cards.title: 1.1.4 Unit Conversions
body: Units are multiplied and divided just like ordinary algebraic symbols.

lessons.title: Errors in Measurement and Significant Figures

cards.title: 1.2.1 Error, Accuracy and Precision
body: **Measurement** is the foundation of all experimental science and technology.
The result of every measurement by any measuring instrument contains some uncertainty.
Every calculated quantity which is based on measured values also has an error.
Systematic errors occur due to an improperly calibrated instrument or bias on the part of an observer.

cards.title: 1.2.2 Scientific Notation
body: Many quantities that scientists deal with have very large or very small values.
For example, the distance travelled by light in one year is 9 461 000 000 000 000 m.
Very small and very large numbers are best expressed with the help of scientific notation or powers of 10 notation.
Numbers expressed as some powers of 10 multiplied by a number between 1 and 10 are said to be in scientific notation.

cards.title: 1.2.3 Significant Figures
body: Normally, the reported result of measurement is a number that includes all digits in the number that are known reliably plus the first digit that is uncertain.
The reliable digits plus the first uncertain digit are known as significant digits or significant figures.
The length of an object reported after measurement to be 367.5 cm has four significant figures, the digits 3, 6, 7 are certain while the digit 5 is uncertain.

Clearly, reporting the result of measurement that includes more digits than the significant digits is unnecessary and also misleading since it would give a wrong idea about the precision of measurement.

cards.title: 1.2.4 Rounding off Numbers
body: The result of computations with approximate numbers which contain more than one uncertain digit, should be rounded off.
The rules for rounding off numbers to the appropriate significant figures are obvious in most cases.
The calculated area and the volume should therefore be rounded off to 4 significant figures.
Express its density by keeping the proper significant figures.

cards.title: 1.2.5 Dimensions of Physical Quantities
body: The dimensions of a physical quantity are the powers (or exponents) to which the base quantities are raised to represent that quantity.
For example, the volume occupied by an object is expressed as the product of length, breadth and height, or three lengths.

Dimensional Formulae and Dimensional Equations The expression which shows how and which of the base quantities represent the dimensions of a physical quantity is called the dimensional formula of the given physical quantity.

cards.title: 1.3.1 Representation of Vectors
body: The magnitude of a vector quantity is printed in italic type (v is the magnitude of the velocity v).
When vector quantities are added, their directions must be taken into account.
Concurrent vectors: If all vectors such as, for example, forces may act at one point of an object, then such forces are said to be concurrent.
Coplanar vectors: If all vectors, for example, forces are in one plane, then the vectors are called **coplanar**.

cards.title: 1.3.2 Position and Displacement Vectors
body: Since the initial and final positions coincide, the displacement is a “null vector”.
Vectors, by definition, obey the triangle law or equivalently, the parallelogram law of addition.
Since, in this procedure of vector addition, vectors are arranged head to tail; this graphical method is called the **head-totail method**.
The two vectors and their resultant form three sides of a triangle, so this method is also known as triangle method of vector addition.

cards.title: 1.3.3 Addition and Subtraction of Vectors – Graphical Method
body: The lengths of the line segments representing these vectors are proportional to the magnitude of the vectors.
The addition of vectors also obeys the associative law .
Subtraction of vectors can be defined in terms of the addition of vectors.
The resultant vector R is directed from the common origin O along the diagonal (OS) of the parallelogram.

cards.title: 1.3.4 Resolution of Vectors
body: If vectors A and B are together equivalent to vector C, then vector C is equivalent to two vectors A and B.
When a vector is replaced by two vectors (in a plane, for example, xy-plane), the process is called **resolving the vector**, and the new vectors are called the components of the initial vector.
The components into which a vector is resolved are nearly always chosen to be perpendicular to one another.
The force F may be resolved into two component vectors Fx and Fy, where Fx is horizontal component of F and Fy is vertical component of F.

glossary.meaning: Length is the fundamental or base quantity used to measure distance or dimension in space.
Mass is the amount of matter an object contains.
Density is a measure of the compactness of the mass of an object.
Measurement is an inseparable part of physics.

tips.text: A Physical quantity is any quantity that can be measured.
Physical quantities are classified into fundamental (base) and derived physical quantities.

Each base quantity is defined in terms of a certain basic, arbitrarily chosen but properly standardised reference standard called a unit (such as metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela).
The units for the fundamental or base quantities are called fundamental or base units.
Physical quantities derived from the base quantities can be expressed as a combination of the base units and are called derived units.
A complete set of units, both fundamental and derived, is called a system of units.
The International System of Units (SI) based on seven base units is, at present, the internationally accepted unit system and is widely used throughout the world.
The SI units have well-defined and internationally accepted unit symbols (such as m for metre, kg for kilogram, s for second, A for ampere, N for newton).
Measurement is an inseparable part of physics.

Small lengths may be measured using a metre rule, vernier callipers, and micrometre screw gauge; beam balances are used for measuring masses; and stopwatches and stopclocks are used for measuring time.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of mass?
why: The seven SI base units include the metre (length), kilogram (mass) and second (time).
The kilogram is the only base unit that already carries a prefix (kilo = 1000), so the base unit is kg, not g.
Answer: kilogram, symbol kg (small k, no plural s).
questions.label: 1. What is the SI unit of mass?
questions.tip: Write kg, never Kg or kgs – capital K is the kelvin.

similar.q: The correct symbol representation for the SI unit of mass is  A) kG.  B) kgs.  C) kg.  D) Kg.  E) Kgs.
similar.a: C. kg. — Unit symbols are never pluralised (no 's') and the prefix 'k' is always small (capital K is kelvin). Answer: C.

questions.q: Is speed a fundamental (base) quantity? Explain.
questions.answer: No – speed is a derived quantity: distance (length) ÷ time.
why: Fundamental quantities cannot be defined from other quantities (length, mass, time, current, temperature, amount, luminous intensity).
Speed = distance ÷ time, so it is built from length and time.
Its unit m/s is made from m and s, so speed is derived, not fundamental.
questions.label: 2. Is speed a fundamental (base) quantity? Explain.
questions.tip: If a quantity's unit is a combination of base units (m/s, kg/m³, N), it is derived.

similar.a: A. meter. — The kilometre, centimetre, millimetre and decimetre are multiples or sub-multiples of the metre, not the base unit. (The centimetre is the length unit of the CGS system.) Answer: A.

questions.q: Write 0.0045 in scientific notation.
why: Scientific notation is a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.
Move the decimal point right until one non-zero digit is in front: 0.0045 → 4.5 (3 places).
Moving right 3 places means n = −3, so 0.0045 = 4.5 × 10⁻³.
questions.label: 5. Write 0.0045 in scientific notation.
questions.tip: Small numbers (less than 1) always have a negative power of ten.

similar.q: Write the number 0.00000436, in scientific notation  A) 436 × 10⁸.  B) 4.36 × 10⁶.  C) 436 × 10⁵.  D) 4.36 × 10⁻⁷.  E) 4.36 × 10⁻⁶.
similar.a: E. 4.36 × 10⁻⁶. — Move the decimal point 6 places to the right to get 4.36, so n = −6: 0.00000436 = 4.36 × 10⁻⁶. Answer: E.

questions.q: How many significant figures are in 0.00450?
why: Leading zeros (0.00…) only place the decimal point – they are not significant.
Non-zero digits 4 and 5 are significant.
A trailing zero after the decimal point is significant, so 0.00450 has 3 significant figures.
questions.label: 6. How many significant figures are in 0.00450?
questions.tip: Count from the first non-zero digit; zeros at the end of a decimal count.

similar.q: The correct prefix to two decimal places of 0.000486 mm is  A) 486 μm.  B) 4.86 μm.  C) 0.49 μm.  D) 0.50 μm.  E) 0.486 μm.
similar.a: C. 0.49 μm. — E is the exact value but has three decimal places; A and B are wrong conversions; D is rounded to one decimal place. Answer: C.

questions.q: Add 12.3 + 0.45 and give the answer to the correct precision.
why: In addition, the answer keeps as many decimal places as the least precise number.
12.3 has 1 decimal place, 0.45 has 2, so the answer gets 1 decimal place.
12.3 + 0.45 = 12.75 → rounded to one decimal place = 12.8.
questions.label: 7. Add 12.3 + 0.45 and give the answer to the correct precision.
questions.tip: Adding/subtracting: count decimal places. Multiplying/dividing: count significant figures.

similar.q: Accuracy vs precision?

questions.q: What is the difference between accuracy and precision?
questions.answer: Accuracy = how close a measurement is to the true value; precision = how close repeated measurements are to each other.
why: Accuracy compares the measurement with the true (accepted) value.
Precision compares repeated readings with one another – small spread means high precision.
Readings can be precise but not accurate (all close together but far from the true value, e.g. a zero error).
questions.label: 8. What is the difference between accuracy and precision?
questions.tip: Think of darts: accurate = near the bull's-eye; precise = darts grouped tightly.

questions.answer: Temperature, mass, time, speed or energy (any one).
why: A scalar has magnitude (size) only, no direction.
Mass (5 kg), time (10 s), temperature (25 °C) and energy (100 J) are complete without a direction.
So any of these is a scalar.
questions.label: 9. Give an example of a scalar quantity.

questions.q: A person walks 10 m east and then 10 m west. What are the distance travelled and the displacement?
why: Distance is the total path length: 10 m + 10 m = 20 m.
Displacement is the change in position from start to finish (a vector).
The person ends where they started, so displacement = 0 m.

similar.a: A. 17. — R = √(8² + 15²) = √(64 + 225) = √289 = 17 N. Answer: A. (23 N would be the sum if they acted in the same direction; 7 N if opposite.)

similar.q: Prefix micro?

questions.q: What power of ten does the prefix micro (µ) stand for?
why: Small prefixes: milli (m) = 10⁻³, micro (µ) = 10⁻⁶, nano (n) = 10⁻⁹.
So 1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m.
Answer: micro = 10⁻⁶.

questions.tip: Each step milli → micro → nano is a further factor of 1000.

similar.q: Why SI?

questions.q: Why do scientists use the SI system of units?
questions.answer: It is agreed worldwide, so results from different countries can be compared.
why: A system of units must be universally agreed and based on reproducible standards.
SI gives one base unit for each fundamental quantity.
Everyone uses the same units, so measurements can be shared and compared without conversion mistakes.
questions.label: 19. Why do scientists use the SI system of units?
questions.tip: SI = Système International – "international" is the key word.

similar.q: Parallax error?
similar.a: Reading a scale from an angle.

questions.q: What is parallax error when reading a scale?
questions.answer: An error caused by reading the scale from an angle instead of straight on.
why: The pointer or liquid surface is a small distance in front of the scale.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: A person walks $$200\text{ m}$$ to the East, then turns around and walks $$60\text{ m}$$ to the West. What is the magnitude of the person's displacement?

steps.text: **Given:** Initial displacement $$x_1 = +200\text{ m}$$ (taking East as positive), subsequent displacement $$x_2 = -60\text{ m}$$ (West).
**Formula:** $$\Delta x = x_1 + x_2$$
**Substitution:** $$\Delta x = 200\text{ m} + (-60\text{ m}) = 140\text{ m}$$.
**Final Result:** The magnitude of the displacement is **$$140\text{ m}$$**.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Zahra travels by car a total distance of $$640\text{ km}$$ in $$8\text{ h}$$. What was her average speed?

steps.text: **Given:** Total distance $$s = 640\text{ km}$$, total time taken $$t = 8\text{ h}$$.
**Formula:** $$v_{av} = \frac{s}{t}$$
**Substitution:** $$v_{av} = \frac{640\text{ km}}{8\text{ h}} = 80\text{ km/h}$$.
**Final Result:** The average speed is **$$80\text{ km/h}$$**.

cards.title: 3.1.1 The Concept of Force
body: A spring balance, a 1 kg mass, a length of spring and a small box.
In physics, a force is a push or a pull exerted by one object on another.
When the wind blows the leaves of a tree, the wind exerts a force.
Forces are physical quantities that can be measured. using a force meter.

cards.title: 3.1.2 Newton’s First Law of Motion
body: When no forces are exerted on an object or when the vector sum of all the forces is zero, the net force is zero.
If an object moves with a constant velocity, then the net force on the object is zero.
The forward force must be equal in size and opposite in direction to the force of friction in order to maintain constant velocity.
If there is no friction, there is no need for a forward force.

cards.title: 3.1.3 Newton’s Second Law of Motion
body: Newton’s first law describes what happens when the net force acting on an object is zero.
In that case, the object either remains at rest or continues to move in a straight line at constant speed.
In other words, an unbalanced force, or net force, accelerates or decelerates.
Newton’s second law involves force, mass, and acceleration.

cards.title: 3.1.4 Newton’s Third Law of Motion
body: Newton’s first and second laws explain how the changes in the motion of a single object changes.
Newton stated that a force applied to one object always comes from another object.
For example, the force of gravity on a falling orange comes from the Earth and the magnetic force acting on a metal nail comes from a magnet.
In other words, one force cannot exist without the other.

cards.title: 3.1.5 Newton’s Law of Universal Gravitation
body: One day Sir Isaac Newton was sitting in his garden and noticed an apple dropped from a tree.
The sight of the falling apple made him think about the problem of motion of the planets.
Newton realised that the force on the apple must be proportional to its mass.
**Gravitational force** is a property of all matter; that is, every object attracts every other object with a gravitational force.

cards.title: 3.1.6 Normal Force
body: The cupboard exerts a downward force on the floor.
According to Newton’s third law of motion, the floor exerts an upward force on the cupboard.
The force that is exerted by a supporting surface on an object that is resting (standing, sitting, lying) on it is called the **normal force**, FN.
**Normal force** is a contact force between two solid objects and acts that is perpendicularly to the contact surfaces (e.g. cupboard and floor).

cards.title: 3.2.1 Friction
body: A ball rolling along the ground gradually slows down and finally comes to rest.
A car also comes to rest once its engine is switched off.
In all these situations no force appears to be acting on the objects, yet their speed gradually decreases and they come to rest after some time.
The force responsible for changing the state of motion of objects is the force of friction.

cards.title: 3.2.2 Advantages and Disadvantages of Friction
body: Car tyres are rough, so they provide high friction and prevent the car from sliding on the road.
A matchstick is lit because of friction.
When a machine is operated, there is friction between moving parts, which causes the parts to wear down and wastes energy.

cards.title: 3.2.3 Methods of Reducing Friction
body: When surfaces are highly polished, there are fewer irregularities and friction decreases.
When oil, grease or graphite is applied between the moving parts of a machine, it forms a thin layer which prevents the moving surfaces from directly rubbing against each other.
The oil reduces the interlocking of irregularities and movement becomes smooth.
The substances which decrease friction are called **lubricants**.

cards.title: 3.2.4 Types of Friction
body: The amount of friction that exists between two bodies depends on the state of each of the bodies, that is whether they are at rest, sliding or rolling.

The frictional force present between two bodies in contact when there is no relative motion between them is called **static friction**, fs.
The force of gravity mg is cancelled by the normal reaction force, FN, of the table.

The larger the value of the coefficient of friction, the larger is the friction present between two surfaces.

questions.q: When can you say that the momentum p of a system is conserved?
questions.answer: When the net external force on the system is zero.

If F_ext = 0, then Δp = 0.

Activities like writing, singing, playing, jumping, running, and cycling require energy.

Machines also require energy to perform work. Therefore, energy is required to perform work.
We cannot imagine our lives without energy.
The sun is the main source of natural energy.
Work, energy and power: W=F s cosθ KE=½mv² PE=mgh P=W/t=Fv Work–energy: net work = ΔKE. Mechanical energy conserved if no heat/friction (school ideal).

questions.q: A force of 20 N moves an object 5 m in its own direction. How much work is done?
why: W = Fs cos θ, with θ = 0° (cos 0° = 1).

similar.q: A 600 J of work is done by a force of 80 N in moving a 4 kg mass along a horizontal surface. The distance moved by the mass in metres is  A) 12.0.  B) 4.8.  C) 7.5.  D) 5.0.  E) 15.0.
similar.a: C. 7.5. — W = Fd (force along the motion, G9 p.203) → d = W/F = 600/80 = 7.5 m. The mass (4 kg) is not needed. Answer: C.

questions.q: A 2 kg mass with 100 J of potential energy at a height of 5 m is dropped. Ignoring air resistance, what is its speed just before it hits the ground? (g = 10 m/s²)
why: Energy is conserved: PE lost = KE gained, so ½mv² = 100 J.

questions.q: A net force of 10 N acts on a 2 kg body at rest over 4 m. Find its kinetic energy and speed.
why: Work–energy theorem: W_net = ΔKE.
W = Fs = 10 N × 4 m = 40 J, so KE = 40 J (it started at rest).
questions.label: 8. A net force of 10 N acts on a 2 kg body at rest over 4 m. Find its kinetic energy and speed.

C) momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not conserved.  D) kinetic energy is conserved but momentum is not conserved.  E) neither momentum nor kinetic energy is conserved.
similar.a: B. momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. — C describes an inelastic collision. Answer: B.

questions.q: What does negative work mean?
questions.answer: The force (or its component) acts against the motion and takes energy away, e.g. friction.
why: W = Fs cos θ.
If θ > 90°, cos θ < 0, so W < 0.
The force removes kinetic energy – friction and braking do negative work.
questions.label: 12. What does negative work mean?
questions.tip: Negative work slows things down.

similar.q:
A container with a mass of 5 kg is lifted to a height of 8 m and then returned back to the ground level. The work done by the gravitational force is
[g = 10 m/s²]  A) zero.  B) 400 J.  C) −400 J.  D) −800 J.  E) 800 J.
similar.a: A. zero. — Total work by gravity over the round trip = −400 + 400 = 0: gravity is a conservative force and the net displacement is zero. Answer: A.

questions.q: You carry a bag across a room at constant height. How much work do you do lifting it (vertically)?
questions.answer: Zero – the height does not change, so no work against gravity.
why: Your force on the bag is upward (supporting its weight).
The displacement is horizontal, at 90° to that force.
W = Fs cos 90° = 0.
questions.label: 13. You carry a bag across a room at constant height. How much work do you do lifting it (vertically)?
questions.tip: Work needs movement along the force.

similar.q: A block of mass 12 kg is lifted from the ground to a building of 6 m high. The work done, in joules, to lift the block is [g = 10 m/s²]  A) 720.  B) 72.  C) 60.  D) 600.  E) 200.
similar.a: A. 720. — Work done against gravity = gain in potential energy = mgh (G9 pp.219–223) = 12 × 10 × 6 = 720 J. Answer: A.

questions.q: What does the spring PE formula ½kx² describe?
questions.answer: The elastic energy stored in a spring stretched or compressed by x.
why: Hooke's law: F = kx, so the force grows from 0 to kx.
Work done = area under the F–x graph = ½ × x × kx.
This work is stored as elastic PE = ½kx².
questions.label: 14. What does the spring PE formula ½kx² describe?
questions.tip: Doubling x gives four times the stored energy.

similar.q: Friction turns mechanical energy into?

questions.q: What does friction turn mechanical energy into?
why: Friction opposes the sliding and does negative work.
The lost kinetic energy is not destroyed.
It becomes internal energy – the surfaces warm up.
questions.label: 15. What does friction turn mechanical energy into?
questions.tip: Rub your hands together – friction makes heat.

similar.q: Efficiency = useful/total × 100%. Can efficiency ever be more than 100%?

questions.q: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input × 100%. Can efficiency ever be more than 100%?
questions.answer: No – a machine cannot give out more energy than is put in.
why: Energy is conserved: output ≤ input.
Some energy is always wasted (mostly as heat).
So efficiency < 100% for real machines.
questions.label: 17. Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input × 100%. Can efficiency ever be more than 100%?
questions.tip: An answer above 100% means input and output were swapped.

similar.q: Machine with 400 J in 100 J useful?

why: Efficiency = useful output ÷ input × 100%.

questions.tip: The other 300 J is wasted energy.

similar.q: Climb 10 m, m=50 kg, t=20 s. Power against gravity?

questions.q: A 50 kg person climbs 10 m in 20 s. What power do they develop against gravity? (g = 10 m/s²)
why: Work against gravity W = mgh = 50 × 10 × 10 = 5000 J.
questions.label: 19. A 50 kg person climbs 10 m in 20 s. What power do they develop against gravity? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.tip: Running up the same stairs faster needs more power, not more work.

similar.q: A motorboat of mass 1000 kg accelerates uniformly from rest to 72 km/h in 20 s. The power output of the motorboat, in kW, is  A) 10.  B) 20.  C) 30.  D) 40.  E) 50.
similar.a: A. 10. — Average power = W/t = 200 000 / 20 = 10 000 W = 10 kW (G9 p.234). Answer: A.

questions.q: A ball is thrown straight up from the ground (no air resistance). Compare its energy at the top with its energy at launch.
questions.answer: At the top it is all PE (v = 0); the total equals the launch KE.
why: Total mechanical energy KE + PE stays constant.
At launch (h = 0) the energy is all KE.
At the peak v = 0, so the energy is all PE: mgh_max = ½mu².
questions.label: 20. A ball is thrown straight up from the ground (no air resistance). Compare its energy at the top…
questions.tip: KE + PE = constant when only gravity does work.

similar.q: Reference of PE?
similar.a: You choose h=0. Only ΔPE matters.

questions.q: Where is the zero (reference level) of gravitational PE?
questions.answer: Wherever you choose (h = 0); only changes in PE matter.
why: PE = mgh measures h from a chosen level.
Changing the level adds the same constant to every PE.
Differences (ΔPE = mgΔh) are unchanged, and only these matter.
questions.label: 21. Where is the zero (reference level) of gravitational PE?
questions.tip: Choose h = 0 at the lowest point to avoid negative numbers.

similar.q: Joule in base units?

questions.q: Express the joule in base SI units.
why: W = Fs, so J = N × m.
N = kg·m/s².
J = kg·m/s² × m = kg·m²/s².
questions.label: 22. Express the joule in base SI units.
questions.tip: Check with KE = ½mv²: kg × (m/s)² = kg·m²/s² ✓.

similar.q: Watt?

questions.q: What is one watt?
questions.answer: One joule per second (1 W = 1 J/s).
why: Power = energy transferred ÷ time.
Units: J ÷ s.
questions.label: 23. What is one watt?

similar.q: Work by gravity on a closed loop back to start?

questions.q: What is the work done by gravity on an object that moves round a closed path back to its start?
questions.answer: Zero – gravity is a conservative force.
why: Work by gravity = −mgΔh.
Back at the start, Δh = 0.
So the total work by gravity is 0 (whatever the path).
questions.label: 24. What is the work done by gravity on an object that moves round a closed path back to its start?
questions.tip: Friction is not conservative – it always does negative work round a loop.

similar.q: Area under F–s graph?

questions.q: What does the area under a force–displacement (F–s) graph give?
why: For a constant force, W = F × s – a rectangle on the F–s graph.
For a changing force, split the area into strips; each is F × Δs.
Total area = total work done.
questions.label: 25. What does the area under a force–displacement (F–s) graph give?
questions.tip: Area under F–s = work; area under v–t = displacement.

similar.q: How do you find the work done by a force that varies?
similar.a: Triangle ½F_max s if linear from 0.

questions.q: A force increases steadily from 0 to F_max over a displacement s. How do you find the work done?
questions.answer: Use the area of the triangle under the F–s graph: W = ½F_max s.
why: A varying force: work = area under the F–s graph.
For a straight line from 0, the shape is a triangle.
W = ½ × base × height = ½ × s × F_max.
questions.label: 26. A force increases steadily from 0 to F_max over a displacement s. How do you find the work done?
questions.tip: The same idea gives spring energy ½kx².

similar.q: Set ½mv² = mgh and solve for v.

questions.q: Set ½mv² = mgh and solve for v.
why: Divide both sides by m: ½v² = gh.
Multiply by 2: v² = 2gh.
Take the square root: v = √(2gh).
questions.label: 27. Set ½mv² = mgh and solve for v.
questions.tip: Mass cancels – all objects falling from the same height reach the same speed (no air).

similar.q: Trap: is any work (W = Fs) done when you hold a bag that does not move?
similar.a: s=0 so W=0 even if you tire (physiology ≠ this W).

questions.q: Trap: is any work (W = Fs) done when you hold a bag still?
questions.answer: No – s = 0, so W = 0, even though you get tired.
why: W = Fs with s = displacement of the bag.
The bag does not move, so s = 0.
W = 0 J; your tiredness comes from muscles working internally, not from work on the bag.
questions.label: 28. Trap: is any work (W = Fs) done when you hold a bag still?
questions.tip: Physics work ≠ effort.

similar.q: Trap: can you add KE and PE if they are in different units?

questions.q: Can you add KE and PE? Are they in the same units?
questions.answer: Yes – both are energies measured in joules.
why: KE = ½mv²: kg × m²/s² = J.
PE = mgh: kg × m/s² × m = J.
Same unit, so KE + PE = total mechanical energy.
questions.label: 29. Can you add KE and PE? Are they in the same units?
questions.tip: Only quantities with the same unit can be added.

similar.q: A stone of mass 0.200 kg is moving with a speed of 5 m/s. The kinetic energy of the stone, in joules, is  A) 8.5.  B) 5.0.  C) 2.5.  D) 9.0.  E) 4.5.
similar.a: C. 2.5. — KE = ½ × 0.200 × 5² = 0.1 × 25 = 2.5 J. Answer: C. (5.0 J forgets the ½.)

questions.q: To find only a final speed, should you use a = F/m with suvat, or energy?
questions.answer: Energy is usually shorter – it skips finding a and t.
why: The energy method links speed directly to height or work: ½mv² = mgh or W = ΔKE.
Newton + suvat needs a = F/m first, then v² = u² + 2as.
Both give the same answer; energy needs fewer steps when time is not needed.
questions.label: 30. To find only a final speed, should you use a = F/m with suvat, or energy?
questions.tip: No time asked, no direction changes? Try energy first.

similar.q: What is the SI unit of force?  A) kg  B) N  C) J  D) W

questions.q: What is the SI unit of force?
why: Force is measured in newtons (N).
1 N = 1 kg·m/s² (from F = ma).
kg is mass, J is energy and W is power, so the answer is B.
questions.tip: N = force, J = energy/work, W = power.

similar.q: An object is dropped from rest from a height of 5 m (g = 10 m/s²). How long does it take to reach the ground?  A) 5 s  B) 0.5 s  C) 1 s  D) 10 s

questions.q: An object is dropped from rest from a height of 5 m (g = 10 m/s²). How long does it take to reach the ground?
why: Dropped from rest: s = ½gt².
5 m = ½ × 10 m/s² × t² = 5t², so t² = 1.
t = 1 s – answer C.
questions.tip: Check: v = gt = 10 m/s, average 5 m/s × 1 s = 5 m ✓.

similar.q: How much work does a force do when it acts at 90° to the displacement?  A) Maximum  B) mgh  C) ½mv²  D) Zero

questions.q: How much work does a force do when it acts at 90° to the displacement?
why: W = Fs cos θ.
W = 0 – answer D.
questions.tip: Perpendicular force → zero work (e.g. a satellite's gravity in circular orbit).

similar.q: When is the total momentum p of a system conserved?  A) Friction is huge  B) Net external force is zero  C) Always, no conditions  D) Only if at rest
similar.a: B. Net external force is zero

questions.q: When is the total momentum p of a system conserved?
why: Δp = F_ext × Δt.
If the net external force is zero, Δp = 0 and total momentum is constant.
Friction (A) would change it, and "always" (C) ignores the condition – answer B.
questions.tip: Conservation of momentum needs zero net external force.
